title: Is This Specimen Worth Testing? Acceptability and Transport
summary: Screen sputum for oral contamination, pick the right CSF tube, swab and transport temperature, and apply the C. difficile formed-stool and three-day stool-culture rules.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 66 Hit 2 (CSF tube 1), Hit 4 (sputum screening), Hit 5 (gonorrhea transport), Hit 7 (urine transport), Hit 8 (three-day rule), Hit 9 (C. difficile formed stool), Hit 10 (pertussis swabs), Hit 14 (anaerobic transport) and Traps 1, 4, 5. Checked against Baron 2013 (IDSA/ASM guide; the 2018 and 2024 updates were read as abstracts only), Dong 2026, Fraij 2020 and the CDC pertussis PCR best-practices page. Hit 4’s “acceptable if < 25 epithelial cells” contradicts its own > 10 rejection rule (register flag rv-sputum-criteria). Hit 7 says “within 2 hours”; Baron 2013 says refrigerate or use a transport tube unless delivery within 1 hour is certain. Hit 5’s “never refrigerate” applies to culture; NAAT devices follow the manufacturer. Not taught: the ≥ 3 unformed stools/24 h and age < 2 C. difficile criteria and the urine colony-count thresholds (not in the sources read in full).

objectives: Screen a sputum Gram stain for oropharyngeal contamination.
Choose the CSF tube, swab type and transport temperature for common microbiology specimens.
Apply the formed-stool rule for C. difficile testing and the three-day rule for stool culture.
Explain why a poor specimen should be rejected and recollected rather than tested.

scenes.title: The morning specimen bin
scenes.altText: A specimen bin slides in. Items pop out one by one: a sputum cup, four numbered CSF tubes, a formed stool labeled “C. difficile”, a gonorrhea culture swab taken from the refrigerator, a cotton swab labeled “pertussis PCR”, and an anaerobic wound vial. Two bins wait: “Accept” and “Reject / recollect”. The cartoon scientist holds a clipboard.

cues.text: The morning bin arrives in microbiology: sputum, spinal fluid, stool, swabs.
Every one of them will be tested only if it is the right specimen, in the right container, at the right temperature, and on time.
A poor specimen gives a misleading result, which is worse than no result. So which of these should be tested, and which recollected?

scenes.title: Sputum: is it lung or spit?
scenes.altText: Two schematic low-power fields of a sputum Gram stain, drawn as boxes with “SEC” (squamous epithelial cell) and “PMN” (neutrophil) tokens. In the first field, many squamous epithelial cells (from the mouth) and few neutrophils: a counter reads “SEC 18 / LPF · WBC 5” → reject: saliva. In the second field, few squamous cells and many neutrophils: “SEC 4 / LPF · WBC 40” → accept: deep sputum. A rule card: acceptable = < 10 SEC and > 25 WBC per low-power field; > 10 SEC = oropharyngeal contamination.

cues.text: Expectorated sputum passes through the mouth, so the lab screens it before culture. A Gram stain is read under the low-power objective.
Squamous epithelial cells are big flat cells from the mouth. Many of them mean the cup holds mostly saliva.
Here there are 18 squamous cells per low-power field and few white cells. This is spit. Culture would grow mouth flora, so it is rejected.
The second sample has 4 squamous cells and 40 white cells per field. That came from the lung, and it is cultured.
One published rule: accept fewer than 10 squamous cells with more than 25 white cells per low-power field; reject more than 10 squamous cells.

props.title: Acceptable: < 10 SEC and > 25 WBC per LPF

scenes.title: Right tube, right swab, right temperature
scenes.altText: The sorting bins fill. CSF: tube 1 has the most skin-flora contamination → not to microbiology; later tubes go. Urine: refrigerate at 4 °C or use a urine transport tube unless it reaches the lab within 1 hour. Anaerobes: anaerobic transport vial at room temperature. Gonorrhea culture: Amies charcoal swab at room temperature (NAAT: the manufacturer’s device, room temperature up to 2 days). Pertussis PCR: posterior nasopharyngeal swab with a polyester (Dacron), rayon or nylon-flocked tip, or an aspirate; cotton and calcium alginate swabs inhibit PCR; throat and anterior nasal swabs are unacceptable.

cues.text: Spinal fluid comes in three or four tubes. The first tube carries the most skin flora from the needle track, so it does not go to microbiology.
Urine is a culture medium in a cup. Refrigerate it, or use a preservative transport tube, unless it will reach the lab within an hour.
Not every specimen should be chilled. Anaerobic specimens travel in an anaerobic transport vial at room temperature.
A gonorrhea culture swab travels in Amies charcoal medium at room temperature. Nucleic acid tests follow the manufacturer’s collection device.
For pertussis PCR, use a nasopharyngeal swab with a polyester, rayon or nylon-flocked tip. Cotton and calcium alginate leave residues that inhibit PCR.

keys.label: Not everything goes in the fridge

scenes.title: Stool: the right sample at the right time
scenes.altText: A stool card: C. difficile toxin or NAAT only on diarrheal stool — a formed stool is rejected unless the physician notes ileus. A timeline from admission: day 0 to day 3 (72 h). Community-acquired diarrhea starting within 72 h of admission → stool culture is reasonable. Diarrhea starting after 72 h → routine stool culture only with exceptions (age ≥ 65 with comorbidity, HIV infection, neutropenia, suspected outbreak); otherwise think C. difficile. Back to the bin: formed stool → reject; GC swab from the fridge → recollect; cotton pertussis swab → recollect; sputum → screen.

cues.text: Testing for C. difficile is done only on diarrheal stool. A formed stool is rejected, unless the physician notes an ileus.
Why? Many people carry C. difficile without disease. A positive test on formed stool would label a carrier as infected.
The three-day rule: routine stool culture makes sense for diarrhea that begins within 72 hours of admission.
Diarrhea that starts later is rarely caused by Salmonella or Shigella. Culture only with exceptions, such as age 65 or older with illness, HIV, neutropenia or an outbreak.
Back to the bin: the formed stool and the cotton pertussis swab are rejected, the chilled gonorrhea culture swab is recollected, and the sputum gets screened.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards appear in turn: “Sputum with 15 squamous cells/LPF has bacteria — culture it” (✓ reject: saliva, recollect); “Formed stool is fine for C. difficile” (✓ diarrheal stool only, unless ileus); “Refrigerate every specimen to be safe” (✓ anaerobes and gonorrhea culture travel at room temperature; urine is refrigerated).

cues.text: Trap one: the sputum has 15 squamous cells per field, but bacteria are present, so culture it. No. It is saliva; reject and recollect.
Trap two: formed stool is fine for C. difficile. No. Test only diarrheal stool, unless the physician notes ileus.
Trap three: refrigerate everything to be safe. No. Anaerobic and gonorrhea culture specimens travel at room temperature; urine is the one to chill.

props.title: ✗ “15 SEC/LPF, but bacteria seen — culture it.”
✗ “Formed stool is fine for C. difficile.”
✗ “Refrigerate every specimen to be safe.”
lines: ✓ Anaerobes and GC culture: room temperature · urine: chill

scenes.title: Right spot, right swab, right temp, right time
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Right spot, right swab, right temp, right time.” Four tokens: spot = deep sputum, CSF after tube 1; swab = polyester/rayon/flocked for PCR; temp = room temperature for anaerobes and GC culture, 4 °C for urine; time = 3-day rule, urine ≤ 1 h. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: right spot, right swab, right temp, right time. Deep sputum and later CSF tubes; PCR-friendly swabs; room temperature or fridge as required; and the clock, from one hour for urine to the three-day rule.
Where it breaks: each lab sets its own acceptance criteria; molecular devices have their own storage rules; there are exceptions such as ileus or an outbreak; and sputum scoring systems vary.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Sputum: < 10 SEC + > 25 WBC/LPF · CSF tube 1 not to micro · C. diff: diarrheal stool only · 3-day rule”, “Urine 4 °C unless ≤ 1 h · anaerobes and GC culture at RT · pertussis PCR: no cotton or alginate”.

cues.text: Test only specimens that represent the infection and survived transport: deep sputum, later CSF tubes, diarrheal stool, chilled urine, room-temperature anaerobes and gonorrhea cultures, and PCR-friendly swabs.

props.label: Sputum < 10 SEC + > 25 WBC/LPF · CSF tube 1 not to micro · C. diff: diarrheal stool · 72 h rule
Urine 4 °C unless ≤ 1 h · anaerobes and GC culture at RT · pertussis PCR: no cotton/alginate

explanation.what: Plain language: a lab result is only as good as the specimen; spit is not sputum, the first CSF tube carries skin bacteria, and some organisms die in the fridge while others overgrow at room temperature. Scientific terms: squamous epithelial cells (SEC) per low-power field (LPF), oropharyngeal contamination, anaerobic transport, Amies charcoal medium, NAAT, PCR inhibition, nosocomial diarrhea, three-day rule.
explanation.why: Squamous cells mark oral contamination; neutrophils mark lower-airway inflammation. Urine supports bacterial growth after collection, inflating counts. Cotton and calcium alginate residues inhibit PCR. Asymptomatic C. difficile carriage makes testing of formed stool misleading. Enteric bacterial pathogens rarely start causing diarrhea after 72 hours in hospital.
explanation.measure: Sputum: acceptable < 10 SEC and > 25 WBC per LPF; reject > 10 SEC/LPF (one published rule). Urine: 4 °C or transport tube unless in lab ≤ 1 h. Anaerobes: anaerobic transport, room temperature. GC culture: Amies charcoal, room temperature; GC NAAT: manufacturer device, room temperature up to 2 days. Pertussis PCR: posterior NP swab (polyester, rayon, nylon-flocked) or aspirate. Stool culture: onset ≤ 72 h after admission, or later only with exceptions.
explanation.differs: Culture vs NAAT transport (viability vs nucleic acid); community-onset vs hospital-onset diarrhea; formed vs diarrheal stool.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: reject a sputum with many squamous cells, which CSF tube goes to micro, refrigerated anaerobic or gonococcal culture specimens, formed stool for C. difficile, and stool culture after 3 days in hospital.

right.label: NAAT
points: Manufacturer device, RT up to 2 days

mnemonic.text: Right spot, right swab, right temp, right time.
mnemonic.explanation: Collect the representative specimen, with the right device, at the right temperature, and within the time limit.
mnemonic.limitation: Each lab sets its own acceptance criteria; molecular devices have their own storage rules; there are exceptions such as ileus or an outbreak; sputum scoring systems vary.

takeaway: Test only specimens that represent the infection and survived transport: deep sputum, later CSF tubes, diarrheal stool, chilled urine, room-temperature anaerobes and gonorrhea cultures, and PCR-friendly swabs.

questions.stem: An expectorated sputum Gram stain shows 18 squamous epithelial cells and 30 neutrophils per low-power field. What should the laboratory do?

options.text: Reject it and request a new specimen
options.rationale: Correct. More than 10 squamous cells per LPF indicates oropharyngeal contamination.

options.text: Culture it because neutrophils are present
options.rationale: Incorrect. Neutrophils do not cancel heavy oral contamination; culture would grow mouth flora.
Incorrect. The specimen is still mostly saliva; changing the culture does not fix the source.

options.text: Refrigerate it for 24 hours and re-read
options.rationale: Incorrect. Waiting does not change the source of the specimen.

questions.stem: Four CSF tubes are collected by lumbar puncture. Which statement about sending them to microbiology is correct?

options.text: Do not send tube 1 for smear and culture; use a later tube
options.rationale: Correct. The first tube has the highest chance of skin-flora contamination.

options.text: Send tube 1 because it is collected first and freshest
options.rationale: Incorrect. Tube 1 carries the most skin flora.
Incorrect. CSF for bacterial culture travels at room temperature, promptly.

options.text: Pool the tubes into one container
options.rationale: Incorrect. Pooling mixes the contaminated first tube into the others.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old inpatient without HIV or neutropenia develops diarrhea on hospital day 6; there is no outbreak. A routine bacterial stool culture is ordered. What is the best response?

options.text: Decline the routine culture under the three-day rule and suggest C. difficile testing on diarrheal stool
options.rationale: Correct. Onset > 72 h after admission without an exception makes Salmonella, Shigella or Campylobacter unlikely.

options.text: Perform the culture; all diarrhea needs culture
options.rationale: Incorrect. Hospital-onset diarrhea rarely yields enteric bacterial pathogens.

options.text: Test a formed stool for C. difficile
options.rationale: Incorrect. C. difficile testing uses diarrheal stool, not formed stool.
Incorrect. This does not address the requested bacterial culture, which the three-day rule advises against.

claims.text: Sputum acceptable < 10 SEC and > 25 WBC per LPF; > 10 SEC = oropharyngeal contamination; labs must screen sputum.
CSF tube 1 has the most skin-flora contamination and should not go to microbiology.
Urine 4 °C or transport tube unless ≤ 1 h; anaerobes in anaerobic transport at RT; GC culture Amies charcoal at RT; GC NAAT in device, RT up to 2 days.
Pertussis PCR: posterior NP swab (polyester, rayon, nylon-flocked) or aspirate; cotton/alginate inhibit PCR; throat and anterior nasal unacceptable.
C. difficile testing on diarrheal stool only, unless ileus; three-day rule with exceptions.
C. difficile testing only with ≥ 3 unformed stools/24 h, no laxatives, no routine testing under age 2; ≥ 10⁵ CFU/mL UTI threshold; cotton is toxic to B. pertussis in culture.

accuracyFlags.issue: Hit 4 rejects sputum with > 10 SEC/LPF but then calls it acceptable with “< 25 epithelial cells AND > 25 neutrophils”, which contradicts itself; Dong 2026 uses < 10 SEC with > 25 leukocytes. The lesson teaches < 10.
